lessons.title: Power BI Dashboard Tutorial — Full Project with DAX
objectives: Write measures that calculate correctly in every context
Build the time comparisons every report needs
Debug a number that looks wrong
lessons.notes:
DAX is the formula language that turns a model into a report. The idea that trips everyone at first is CONTEXT: a measure does not have one answer, it recalculates for wherever it appears - this month, this county, this product - and understanding that is the whole skill.

MEASURES VERSUS CALCULATED COLUMNS, and getting this wrong is the commonest beginner mistake. A CALCULATED COLUMN is computed once per row and stored; use it when you need a value to group or filter by, such as a category. A MEASURE is computed on demand for whatever slice is being shown; use it for anything you are aggregating - totals, averages, percentages. Building a calculated column for a total produces a number that does not change when the user filters, which is wrong in a way nobody notices for weeks.

THE HANDFUL THAT COVER MOST WORK: SUM and AVERAGE of a column; COUNTROWS; DIVIDE, which handles division by zero properly and should always be used instead of a slash; CALCULATE, which is how you change the filters a measure sees; and the time intelligence functions for the same period last year and for a running total.

TIME COMPARISONS ARE WHAT REPORTS ARE ACTUALLY FOR. This month against last, this year to date against last year to date. They need a proper date table, which is why Module 2 built one.

WHEN A NUMBER LOOKS WRONG: check the relationship direction first, then whether you used a column where a measure was needed, then whether a filter is doing something you did not intend. In that order, because that is the frequency order too.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - two habits worth more than more DAX. RECONCILE ONE NUMBER BY HAND before you show the report, every time - take one month, one branch, one product and add it up from the source. A report with one verified figure is trusted; a report that turns out to be wrong once is never trusted again, and rebuilding that trust costs far more than the check. Second, WRITE MEASURES THE CLIENT'S ACCOUNTANT WOULD RECOGNISE and name them in their words - if the business says gross margin and means something specific, define it their way and say so on the page. A technically correct measure that disagrees with the figure the owner has in their head produces an argument you will lose even when you are right, so surface the definition rather than burying it.
lessons.practice: Build four measures on real data - a total, an average, a percentage using DIVIDE, and the same period last year - and one calculated column, writing down why each is a measure or a column. Then reconcile one month by hand against the source, and write the definition of your main measure in the client's own words on the report page.

quiz.question: When should a calculated column be used instead of a measure?
options: When you need a value to group or filter by, such as a category
When the report has no filters

quiz.question: What should be checked first when a number looks wrong?
options: The relationship direction, then column-versus-measure, then the filters

lessons.title: Storytelling with Data (Crash Course)
objectives: Lead with the finding rather than the method
Structure an analysis so a decision follows from it
Present to someone who will not read a report
lessons.notes:
Analysis that nobody acts on has failed, however good it was. The difference is almost never the quality of the work; it is how it was presented.

LEAD WITH THE FINDING. Not the data source, not the method, not a tour of the charts. One sentence saying what is true and what should be done about it, and then the evidence for anyone who wants it. Analysts consistently do this backwards because the work felt like the important part.

THE STRUCTURE THAT PRODUCES A DECISION: what we found, why it matters in money or risk, what we recommend, what we are unsure about. That last one is not weakness - naming your uncertainty is what makes the rest credible.

ONE MESSAGE PER CHART, and say the message in the title. A reader who sees only your titles should get the whole argument.

CUT RUTHLESSLY. The analysis you did is not the analysis you present. Nobody needs the six things you checked that turned out to be nothing, and including them buries the one that mattered.

KNOW YOUR AUDIENCE: an owner wants the decision, a manager wants the decision and the cause, a technical colleague wants the method. Sending all three the same document serves none of them.

BE HONEST ABOUT WHAT THE DATA CANNOT SAY. Correlation, small samples, a month that was unusual for a known reason. An analyst who says where the evidence is thin is believed about everything else.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - presenting to the people you will actually present to here. MOST OF YOUR AUDIENCE WILL NOT OPEN A REPORT. Put the finding and the number in the WhatsApp message, in shillings, in one sentence, and attach the detail for anyone who wants it - that single habit does more for whether your work is used than any chart. Second, EXPECT TO PRESENT IN PERSON AND BE INTERRUPTED: prepare to give the whole thing in two minutes standing up, because that is often what you get. Third, BE CAREFUL WITH DATA THAT NAMES PEOPLE OR PLACES - survey results by village, performance by named staff member, health data by facility - because a finding that identifies someone can do real harm when forwarded, and it will be forwarded. Aggregate to a level that answers the question without exposing individuals, and say in the report what you aggregated and why.
lessons.practice: Take an analysis you have done and rewrite the delivery: one sentence with the finding and the recommendation, then the evidence. Retitle every chart with its message and cut everything that answers no question. Then write the one-sentence WhatsApp version in shillings, and practise giving the whole thing in two minutes.

quiz.question: What should an analysis lead with?
options: The finding and what should be done about it

quiz.question: Why name what the data cannot say?
options: An analyst who says where the evidence is thin is believed about everything else

lessons.title: End-to-End Data Analytics Project (Python + SQL)
objectives: Take a project from raw data to a stated conclusion
Use SQL and Python for the parts each does best
Document the work so someone else can check it
lessons.notes:
This is the long applied project, and it is the thing you will show an employer. WATCH IT IN PARTS across several sessions with the work open beside you - it is long, and streaming it in one sitting costs real money on a bundle.

THE SHAPE OF A REAL PROJECT:
THE QUESTION, written down before you touch the data, in one sentence. Projects without one wander and produce a folder of charts instead of an answer.
GET THE DATA and record where it came from and when.
EXPLORE IT before cleaning: how many rows, what date range, what is missing, what looks impossible. Most findings start here.
CLEAN IT, recording every decision - what you dropped and why, what you did with blanks and duplicates.
ANALYSE, which is usually far less code than beginners expect.
CONCLUDE, in a sentence, with the uncertainty named.

WHAT SQL AND PYTHON EACH DO BEST: SQL for pulling and aggregating from a database, because that is what it is for and it is faster; Python for the cleaning, reshaping and charting afterwards. Use both rather than forcing everything into one.

DOCUMENT AS YOU GO in the notebook itself. A future reader - an employer, a colleague, you in three months - needs to know what you did and why, not just the code. A project with a clear written narrative is worth several with only code.

CHECK YOUR OWN RESULT before concluding. Take one number and verify it a different way.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - use data from here, because it is both more persuasive and better practice. Kenyan open data, county and national statistics, published survey microdata, and anything you can collect yourself are all real and all messier than a tutorial dataset - which is the point, since handling a genuinely awkward file is the skill an employer is hiring for. A project answering a question about your own county, market or sector will be read by a local employer with far more interest than another analysis of a famous foreign dataset. Two cautions: STATE YOUR SOURCE AND ITS DATE, because official figures get revised; and be careful with anything identifying individuals or small groups - aggregate before you publish, and do not put a dataset containing personal information in a public portfolio repository.
lessons.practice: Choose a real question about somewhere or something you know, and work the whole shape - question, source, explore, clean, analyse, conclude - in parts over several sessions. Record every cleaning decision in the notebook. Verify one key number a second way, and write the conclusion in one sentence with its uncertainty named.

quiz.question: What must be written down before touching the data?
Why use Kenyan data for a portfolio project?
options: It is messier, which is the real skill, and a local employer reads it with more interest

lessons.title: Build a Complete Power BI Dashboard Project
objectives: Deliver a full Power BI report as a finished piece of work
Design for the person who will use it, not for yourself
Hand it over so it survives without you
lessons.notes:
The final Power BI build. Do the tutorial, then do it again with data from a real organisation you know - the second one is the portfolio piece and the first is practice.

THE ORDER, and departing from it costs you a rebuild: connect, transform properly, model with relationships and a date table, write the measures, then build the visuals. Everyone wants to start at the visuals and everyone who does rebuilds them.

DESIGN FOR THE READER. One page that answers the main questions, with detail pages behind it for people who want to dig. The most important number large and top left. Slicers grouped together and clearly labelled. Consistent colours with one meaning per colour.

MAKE THE FILTERS OBVIOUS. A reader who does not notice a filter is on will read a subset as the whole, and blame the report when they discover it - so show the active filter state on the page.

PERFORMANCE MATTERS more than tutorials suggest. Remove the columns you are not using, avoid stacking calculated columns where a measure would do, and keep the model tidy. A report that takes a minute to load is a report nobody opens twice.

HAND IT OVER PROPERLY: where the data comes from, how often it refreshes, what each measure means in the business's words, and what to do when it breaks. A report nobody but you can maintain has a short life.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the practical constraints on delivering Power BI work here. SHARING A POWER BI REPORT PROPERLY REQUIRES A PAID LICENCE PER VIEWER in foreign currency, which many small clients will not sustain - so know your options before promising anything: export to PDF for a fixed report, take screenshots for a WhatsApp update, or rebuild in a free browser tool for something the client will open themselves. Say this at the quoting stage rather than after the build. Second, REFRESH IS A DEPENDENCY: if the source is a file on your machine, the report dies the day you stop updating it, so put the source somewhere the client controls and can keep feeding. Third, ASK WHO WILL ACTUALLY OPEN THIS AND ON WHAT - if the answer is the owner, on a phone, once a week, then a one-page PDF sent on WhatsApp is the better deliverable and the Power BI work is your internal tool rather than the product.
lessons.practice: Build a complete report in the correct order from real data, with the active filter state visible and the model trimmed of unused columns. Then answer the delivery question honestly: work out what it would cost the client to view it properly, and produce the alternative - a one-page PDF - alongside. Write the handover note covering source, refresh and measure definitions.

quiz.question: What does starting at the visuals cost you?
options: A rebuild, because the transform and model change what the visuals can do

quiz.question: What must be settled at quoting stage for Power BI work here?
options: That sharing properly needs a paid licence per viewer, and what the alternative will be

lessons.title: How to Become a Freelance Data Analyst
objectives: Define a service a client will recognise and buy
Find the organisations here that genuinely need analysis
Price and scope data work so it stays profitable
lessons.notes:
Freelance data work is real, and it is sold badly by most people who try it, because they offer analysis and clients do not buy analysis. Clients buy an answer to a question that is costing them something.

WHAT TO OFFER, in the client's words: we do not know which products actually make money; we cannot tell what happened last quarter without three days of work; our reports are rebuilt by hand every month; the data from the field is a mess and unusable.

THE SERVICES THAT SELL, smallest first:
A ONE-OFF ANALYSIS answering a specific question with a written conclusion.
A CLEANING AND STRUCTURING JOB, turning an unusable export into something reliable. Unglamorous and frequently needed.
A DASHBOARD that replaces a monthly manual report. This is the one that recurs, because they need it maintained.
A MONTHLY REPORTING ARRANGEMENT once a dashboard exists.
TRAINING their own staff to keep it running, which pays well and brings referrals.

SCOPE IT BEFORE STARTING. The danger in data work is the question that expands: one more breakdown, one more year, one more source. Agree the question, the sources, the number of revisions, and what a new question costs.

NEVER QUOTE BEFORE SEEING THE DATA. Ask for a sample. Clean and messy differ by several times the work, and the data is always worse than the client believes.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - where the demand actually is here, and it is not where most people look. NGOS AND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMMES have monitoring and evaluation obligations, real budgets, and field data that arrives in poor shape - this is the largest and most reliable source of data work in this market, and monitoring and evaluation is a career path in its own right. Beyond that: research institutes and universities, SACCOs and microfinance, health facilities and county offices, agribusinesses, schools with fee and performance data, and marketing agencies needing campaign reporting. Second, THE FIRST DELIVERABLE THAT CONVINCES ANYONE is a clean, reliable answer to one question they have been arguing about - not a dashboard. Third, on terms: DEPOSIT BEFORE STARTING, on M-Pesa, scope in writing, and be explicit about the DATA you are given - agree what you may do with it, keep it somewhere access-controlled, and say when you will delete it, because much of this work involves personal information and that is your responsibility under the Data Protection Act as much as theirs.
lessons.practice: Write your offer in three client sentences rather than as a service list. Then list fifteen organisations near you that clearly generate data - NGOs, SACCOs, clinics, schools, agribusinesses - and approach three, asking for a sample of their data before quoting anything.

quiz.question: What do clients actually buy?
options: An answer to a question that is costing them something, not analysis

quiz.question: Where is the most reliable data work in this market?
options: NGOs and development programmes with monitoring and evaluation obligations

lessons.title: 3 Data Analyst Portfolio Projects to Get Hired
objectives: Build projects that show judgement rather than tool use
Write each one up so a hiring manager reads it
Choose subjects that make you memorable here
lessons.notes:
A portfolio of three good projects beats ten mediocre ones, and what makes a project good is almost never the technique.

WHAT A HIRING MANAGER IS LOOKING FOR: can this person take a vague question and make it answerable, handle messy data without giving up, reach a defensible conclusion, and explain it to someone who is not an analyst. Not whether you can use a particular library.

THE THREE PROJECTS THAT COVER THE GROUND:
A CLEANING AND EXPLORATION PROJECT on genuinely messy real data, where the write-up is mostly about the decisions you made and why.
AN ANALYSIS ANSWERING A SPECIFIC QUESTION, with a conclusion, the evidence for it, and an honest account of the uncertainty.
A DASHBOARD OR REPORT built for a stated audience, with the questions it answers written at the top.

THE WRITE-UP IS THE PROJECT. Code in a repository with no explanation is not a portfolio piece. For each: the question, where the data came from, what was wrong with it, what you decided and why, what you found, what you would do with more time. Short, structured, readable in three minutes.

SHOW ONE THING THAT WENT WRONG in at least one project - a hypothesis that did not hold, a data problem you discovered halfway. It is the most credible thing in any portfolio and almost nobody includes it.

AVOID THE FAMOUS TUTORIAL DATASETS. A hiring manager has seen the same three analyses many times and they demonstrate nothing about you.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - choose subjects that make you memorable to an employer here. USE KENYAN DATA AND A KENYAN QUESTION: county health or education figures, agricultural prices across markets, transport or weather data, published survey microdata, or something you collected yourself in your own town. It is messier, which shows the real skill, and a local employer reads it with genuine interest rather than recognition fatigue. Second, MAKE IT OPENABLE ON A PHONE ON A BUNDLE - a light page or a short PDF beats a heavy notebook nobody loads, and put the finding at the top for the manager who reads only that. Third, BE CAREFUL WITH PERSONAL DATA: never put a dataset containing identifiable individuals in a public repository, aggregate before publishing, and state in the write-up what you aggregated and why - which, incidentally, is itself a signal of professional judgement that hiring managers notice.
lessons.practice: Build the three projects on Kenyan data, each with a written summary of question, source, what was wrong with the data, decisions, findings and uncertainty. Include one thing that went wrong. Then check each opens quickly on a phone, and confirm no published dataset identifies an individual.

quiz.question: What is a hiring manager actually looking for?
options: Whether you can make a vague question answerable and explain the answer to a non-analyst

quiz.question: What is the most credible thing you can include?
options: Something that went wrong - a hypothesis that failed or a problem found halfway
